Station Six: God hears and sees

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. We ask His help. Praise belongs to God, who gives existence to all things through His own necessary existence and shines the light of His own reality on the realities of all that exists and on all that may exist. From the light of His being He brings into existence the lasting realities of the intelligences, and from the showing of His attributes He brings the souls of the heavens into being. He makes the pages of the heavenly and earthly bodies a book of His words. He brings about the causes of motion and the cycles of all that exists, so that His mercy may continue to reach us and His gifts and blessings may be renewed. Among all the forms of existence, He made the human soul ready to bear His trust and His messages. It reveals the wonders of His creation and the strange effects of His works. It carries the book of His signs and reads the clear and hidden meanings in the book He sent down. I thank Him for His abundant gifts, the wisdom and inspiration He gives, the fullness of His kindness, and the light of His proofs. I ask Him to bless Muhammad, His servant and teacher, the bearer of good news and warning, who was given words of great meaning, sent with the truth to give good news and warn, and made, by God's leave, a caller to God and a shining lamp; and to bless his chosen, exalted family, who guard the secrets of revelation and certainty, carry the clear book of truth, and open the way to nearness to the Lord of all worlds.

This begins a new stage in wisdom and knowledge: looking closely at beings as they are and establishing the reality of beings beyond matter and of divine things. This is called knowledge of God and divine wisdom. The greatest gift God gives to His creatures, and the noblest gift He grants to any servant, is what He calls in His illuminating Book “great good”: divine wisdom and knowledge of God. It is surely the greatest happiness and joy. By gaining it, a person reaches great honor and a high standing above all other ranks and forms of excellence.

Whoever receives a gift from God must give thanks and return kindness in keeping with that gift. So anyone whom God has shown mercy, taught from His own knowledge, and given strength in this field—so that he can walk through the land of realities, find light in the darkness of the lower worlds, rise on wings to the heights of the upper worlds, and see the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, as God says He showed Abraham—so that he might be among those who have certainty.

Such a person should hasten to thank God for His favor and generosity. He should make His kindness known, as God commands: “Speak of the blessings of your Lord.” He should also hope for more of God's kindness, as God promises: “If you give thanks, I will give you more.” He should explain these important ideas and uncover these lofty aims so that people may benefit and their lives to come may be set right.

In this field, we see the different ranks people may reach and the states they may attain in the life to come. If someone reaches them, that person has gained the fullest good and the widest perfection. If someone writes them down in a book, the reward will be great and the memory will be honored. Perhaps the book will become a garden inherited by the people who are mindful of God, and its author will be praised by those who come later. Guiding others who seek the truth is one of the greatest ways to draw near to the Lord of all worlds. It is a mark of the messengers, may God's peace be upon our Prophet, his family, and all of them. The revealed books contain many words that show the honor of knowledge and teaching. Among the words revealed to our father Adam is this: “Those who discover knowledge are dearer to Me than those who build up the earth through crafts.”

Whoever discovers knowledge and writes it in a book is like Adam, the chosen one. The Prophet said to Mu'adh: “If God guides one person through you, it is better for you than the world and all it contains.” There are many such sayings, and recounting them all would take too long.

With God's help, we have set out the rules of this field, built its foundations, shown its path and proofs, and revived its teachings after they had faded. We have strengthened what had fallen into ruin. We have established what was true in the philosophers' views and rejected what was false. The early philosophers rarely went wrong in the foundations and main principles, because they followed the path of the prophets. The claims often attributed to them—that the world has always existed, that God has no power, that He does not know particular things, and that there is no bodily resurrection—are all lies told about them and grave falsehoods.

Later philosophers, such as followers of the school of Aristotle and other recent thinkers, have made grave mistakes in divine questions and many natural questions. These are matters where people cannot excuse error and forgetfulness, if they are ready and able to follow the path toward the life to come. Some have gone astray and turned away from the road that leads to their final home.

A wise person does not follow a claim just because it is popular. If the truth opposes the majority, the wise person still accepts it. In every matter, the wise person asks not who said it but what was said. It is reported that our leader, the Commander of the Faithful, said: “You do not know the truth by knowing people. Know the truth, and then you will know its people.” In every question we have examined, our only aim has been to draw near to God and His highest realm by guiding a sincere seeker or refining a clear mind. If careful thinkers agree with us, that is what we hoped for. If they do not, the truth does not always fit minds clouded by inner illnesses that even healers of the soul cannot cure. The guiding Prophet was told by God: “You cannot guide everyone you love.” When people seek wisdom in the wrong way, it only makes them more resistant and proud.

They gain nothing from it and reach no result. They also lose the chance to follow the examples found in revelation and the paths set out by sacred law. They return empty-handed, covered in shame. This is great loss and painful deprivation. A wise person has no words or books for people like this, and no call or address for those like them. God says: “Even if you brought those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your direction.” He also says: “Even if they saw every sign, they would not believe in it.” How could they believe in what they cannot see when they are not ready to do so?

Wisdom and the light of knowledge have conditions and causes. They include an open heart, a sound nature, good character, sound judgment, a sharp mind, quick understanding, and a taste for insight gained through direct spiritual experience. Along with all this, the heart must have a light from God that keeps burning like a lamp. This light guides a person to wisdom, just as a lamp shows what is in a room.

If someone lacks these qualities, let alone God's light, that person should not tire themselves by seeking wisdom. Someone may have understanding but lack direct insight and the light that guides them. Such a person will not gain wisdom, even if they get some parts right and master some of its starting points. “If God gives no one light, that person has no light.”

Know, then, that this part of wisdom, which we are beginning, is its finest part: true faith in God, His signs, and the Last Day. God points to this faith when He says, “The believers—all of them—believe in God, His angels, His Books, and His messengers,” and, “Whoever rejects God, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has gone far astray.” This field contains two noble kinds of knowledge: knowledge of the beginning and knowledge of the return. Knowledge of the beginning includes knowing God, His attributes, His actions, and their effects. Knowledge of the return includes knowing the soul, the Resurrection, and prophecy.

God praises those who look and think about both. He praises those who look at the creation of the world and its wonders, which show the greatness and oneness of its maker: “They reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth and say, ‘Our Lord, You did not create this without purpose.’” He also praises those who look into their own souls and cleanse them of material coverings: “By the soul and the One who formed it, then showed it what is wrong and what is right: successful is the one who purifies it.”

“And lost is the one who buries it.” God condemns those who turn away from reflecting on His wisdom and signs, thinking about the wonders of His creation, and remembering Him. In many places in His noble Book, He says, for example, “If you ask them who created the heavens and earth, they will say, ‘God.’” He condemns them because they did not reach this knowledge through learning and thought, but only copied what they had heard and accepted it without examining it. He also says, “How many signs there are in the heavens and earth that they pass by and turn away from.” God condemns them for turning away from wisdom and reproaches them for refusing to seek the truth of things and the hidden secrets in the worlds of creation and command. He says, “I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and earth or to their own creation, nor do I take those who lead others astray as helpers.” This points out that they lack both kinds of knowledge and are led astray because of it. Those who mislead others have no share in the truth. They went astray and led others astray only after they failed to learn, turned away from knowledge, and grew arrogant. God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves.

Reason and the Qur'an therefore agree: learning divine wisdom and knowing the human soul—that is, learning about the beginning and the return—lead to everlasting life. Rejecting this knowledge leads to lasting loss.

My brothers on this path, I have already offered you lights of wisdom, subtle sayings, basic ideas, general rules, principles for weighing claims, and judgments of the mind. These are steps of great value and ranks on the road to God, which we travel through thought and inspiration. They are stairways to knowledge of God, to seeing the beauty and attributes of the One, to the company of the holy ones and the people of the kingdom and the highest realms. These are the aims of those who receive revelation and of those who uncover its deeper meanings. Their knowledge comes from the angels near to God and the noble recording angels.

These high and noble aims begin with God. He first placed them in the great Pen and the honored Tablet. He taught the Pen what it did not know, spoke to it through His words, inspired it with the clear signs, and guided it with His light. He then chose it and made it His representative on earth, fit for the upper world and a representative of His heavenly kingdom. This knowledge gives a person a vast realm, for it is the greatest elixir: it brings complete richness, the greatest happiness, the best lasting state, likeness to the highest good, and a character shaped by God's qualities.

In one of the revealed books, God says: “Child of Adam, I created you to live forever, and I am the Living who never dies. Obey what I command and avoid what I forbid, and I will make you like Me: living, never to die.” A saying from our Prophet also describes the people of Paradise. When an angel enters their presence, the angel gives them a letter from God after greeting them in His name. It says: “From the Living, the Self-Sustaining, who never dies, to the living, the self-sustaining, who never dies: I say to a thing, ‘Be,’ and it is. Today I have given you the power to say to a thing, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

This is one of the stations a person can reach through wisdom and knowledge. Those who follow the Sufi path call it the station of “Be.” It is said that during the expedition to Tabuk the Prophet said to Abu Dharr, “Be Abu Dharr,” and he became Abu Dharr. There is a station beyond this, called the station of being lost in God's oneness. God points to it in a sacred saying: “When I love someone, I become the hearing with which they hear and the sight with which they see.”

During this journey, the proof will make this clear to you and teach you the knowledge that brings great joy and the highest rank to those who learn it and live by it. Understand it, take it in, and be happy through it. Share it only with those who will live by it. To live by it means to turn away from the world and prepare for the next life through mindfulness of God.

We have made this rough road easier, clearing away its thorns and stones and smoothing its hard places so that any of God's servants who wishes may find the way. God is the giver of grace and guidance. In His hand are the keys to goodness and wisdom, and with Him are the stores of generosity and mercy. This part contains several arts.

I. Establishing God's Existence and Coming to Know Him
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

Know that there are many paths to God, because He has many perfections and can be approached from many sides. Each person turns toward a different direction. Some paths, though, are firmer, nobler, and clearer than others. The strongest and noblest proof does not rely on anything other than God Himself to connect its steps. The way to the goal is then the goal itself. This is the path of the people of truth: they point to God as proof of God, then use His own being to show His attributes, and His attributes to show His actions, one after another. Other people—such as theologians and natural philosophers—try to know God and His attributes through something else: for example, the possibility of an essence, the createdness of the world, or the body's motion. These are also signs of God's being and attributes, but this path is stronger and nobler.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The Qur'an points to both paths. God says, “We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that He is the Real.” He also says, “Is it not enough that your Lord is witness to everything?” The people who know God look at existence itself and understand that it is the source of everything. From there, they see that existence, in its own reality, must exist necessarily. Possibility, need, and dependence on a cause do not belong to existence in itself. They come from its limits and absences.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

By considering what follows from necessary or possible existence, they show that God's being and attributes are one. From His attributes they learn how His actions and effects follow. This is the path of the prophets, as God says: “Say, ‘This is my path: I call to God with clear insight.’” The argument is as follows. As we have explained, existence is one real, simple reality. Its instances differ in themselves only by how complete or limited, strong or weak they are, or by features added to them, as happens among the members of a kind. The fullest existence is the one beyond which there can be nothing more complete: it depends on nothing else, and nothing greater can be imagined. Anything incomplete depends on something else and needs what completes it. We have already shown that completeness comes before lack, actuality before potential, and existence before nonexistence. We have also shown that the completeness of a thing is that thing together with what surpasses it. So existence is either independent of anything else, or, by its very nature, in need of something else.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The first is the Necessary Being: existence in its purest form, beyond which nothing can be more complete, with no lack or imperfection mixed into it. The second is everything else: God's effects and works. Nothing else can stand without Him. As we have already seen, existence itself has no lack. Lack belongs to it because it is an effect. An effect cannot equal its cause in the fullness of existence. If existence were not brought into being and held under the power of a creator, it could not be limited in any way. Existence is simple and has no boundary or identity apart from being fully real and actual. If it were made up of parts or had an essence apart from existence, it would not be simple.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

We have also shown that if an existence is caused, it is made to exist in a single, direct act. In its very being, it depends on the one who brings it into being. So it is now clear: existence is either complete in itself and necessary, or it depends in its very being on the Necessary Being. Either way, the Necessary Being's existence is independent of everything else. That is what we set out to prove.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

This proof is extremely strong. It comes close to the path of the Illuminationists, who begin from the principle of light. But later thinkers, because they overlook some of its steps or cannot grasp how existence can be stronger or weaker, sometimes object to it. At times they say it makes no sense for one reality to differ in perfection and lack while remaining the same reality, as if what makes things alike and what makes them different were one and the same. At other times, they accept that existence differs in degree but deny that completeness belongs to existence itself, or that lack makes a thing dependent on something more complete. They argue: if existence itself made a thing necessary, then every existent would be necessary. If it made a thing possible and dependent, then every existent would be possible. If it did neither, both necessity and possibility would need causes outside existence. Then even the Necessary Being would depend on a cause, which is impossible. Since all three conclusions are false, they say the claim that existence is one reality with degrees of completeness and lack must also be false.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

I say that this objection comes from not understanding the point. The unity of existence is not like the unity of the human essence. The unity of an essence is mental: it belongs to general ideas after the mind sets aside the individual features of particular people. We divide that one idea into different cases by adding different limits: a person is one way or another. Existence, however, is not one general essence shared by everything. So it cannot be divided in the same way as other general ideas, which can exist in the mind and be shared by many things. The mind divides a general kind according to the forms of its members: a broader kind, a species, or an individual. But existence is not a broader kind, a species, or an individual under a broader kind.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The unity and sharing of existence among particular things is a different kind of unity. This objection therefore misses its mark. It would apply only if existence were a general nature. If someone instead means the general idea of “being,” and says that if this idea makes one instance necessary then all must be necessary, we answer: if “being” means the reality of existence, then our claim stands. If it means only the general idea we use when we say that something exists, that idea does not make anything necessary. It is like other features that depend on what they describe. No such feature is the Necessary Being, or even a separate thing in the world outside the mind. Someone may say that the idea of existence is identical with God but added to possible things. This means only that God, considered on His own, is what we point to when we say “exists,” while a possible thing is not, unless we consider it together with its cause.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

A correction and refinement. The Illuminationist writer raised a similar objection against his own path, which is based on light and darkness. His answer, in brief, is this: the common essence found in the perfect, middle, and deficient levels is a general idea in the mind. It is not something shared by them in the outside world. What exists outside the mind is not made of a common essence plus a degree of perfection. Each individual is different from the others. The perfect being is one thing, the deficient being another, and the one between them a third. So their features and effects may differ. The mistake comes from treating what exists in the mind as if it were what exists outside it.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

I say that the truth is that a general nature does exist outside the mind, especially according to those who say existence is only an idea and that the essences of things—not their existence—are what is real. For them, it is the essence of a thing that exists outside the mind. The general nature is not general there as it is in the mind, but it is something that the mind can recognize as shared by many things.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

So the shared feature exists outside the mind, even though the mind is where it becomes a general idea. It is one essential meaning found in things that differ in perfection, lack, and other features. The mind can consider that shared meaning by itself, with or without the mental idea of oneness. It then sees one of two things: either the shared nature itself requires a particular level or feature, in which case everything else falls outside its true instances; or it requires none of them, in which case each level and feature must come from something added to the shared nature.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

This is why it is wrong to say that, when a general essence is shared, the very thing that makes instances different in perfection or lack is also what makes them the same. A general essence is capable of appearing in every instance and every part, and it has a common definition that applies to all of them. If that nature required completeness and strength, then all its instances would be complete and strong. If it required lack and weakness, then they would all be lacking and weak. If it required neither, then each would need some added feature to explain its level. So no essence can be more or less complete, stronger or weaker, except through added features.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

This objection does not apply to existence when existence has different degrees. Existence is not a general idea in the mind that can take different forms of being, as the human or horse essence can. Those essences have one shared definition, which becomes particular through added features, and which the mind can separate from each feature in turn. The reality of existence, as we have learned, is nothing but the particular identities of things. When existence varies in degree—stronger or weaker, earlier or later—it cannot be divided into a shared nature plus an added feature. Its complete level cannot be broken down into a common part and something extra, because its identity is simple.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The weaker level is also just existence; its lack is a kind of absence. So the reality of existence in each thing is according to that thing's own level. The unity that gathers all these levels is neither the unity of a species nor the unity of a broader kind. It is another kind of unity, known only to those who have reached full insight.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The Illuminationist writer would be right if, by the essence of light—which he regards as simple yet varying in strength and weakness—he meant the very reality of existence. But if he meant a general idea that can apply to many things, his claim cannot be made sound. The thinkers in Aristotle’s school say that stronger and weaker shades of black, heat, light, and similar qualities come from the different states of individual things, not from differences in a shared idea. Their view is close to what we have said.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

A brief reminder: the light of truth has dawned through the explanation you have heard, seeker. The reality of existence is simple. It has no separate essence and no part that defines or limits it. It is itself the Necessary Being, whose perfection has no limit. Any level less strong than this is not pure existence; it includes a lack. A thing's lack is not the thing itself. The lack of existence is absence. This absence does not belong to existence simply because it exists. It comes from its place at a lower level, after the first. So lack and need belong to later beings because they come later. The First Being has limitless perfection, beyond which nothing can be more complete. Lack and need arise from the giving of existence, but the gift also completes them: the later beings depend on the First, and their lack is made good by His fullness; their need is met by His independence.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

This proof establishes God's existence and also establishes His oneness. Existence is one reality, and in its own nature it has no lack or division. It also establishes His knowledge of Himself and of everything else, and His life, because knowledge is existence itself. It establishes His power and will, since these follow from life and knowledge. It also shows that His existence sustains everything. The strongest existence gives freely and acts on all that is below it. He is knowing, powerful, willing, living, sustaining, aware, and active. Since the levels that follow Him are ordered from weaker to stronger and from lower to nobler, His creating, bringing things into being, command, kingdom, and rule are also established.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

This path is the surest, noblest, and most direct. A seeker does not need to know God, His attributes, or His actions by first proving something else, nor must the seeker rely on disproving circular causes or an endless chain of causes. God is known through Himself. “God bears witness that there is no god but Him.” Other things are known through Him: “Is it not enough that your Lord is witness to everything?”
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

For those who have reached full understanding, this path is enough to know the truth, its signs, and its works. But not everyone can draw many conclusions from one starting point. So teaching must also explain the other paths that lead to the truth, even if they do not lead to it as directly.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
II. Other Paths to This Great Goal
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

One of these paths is the one we mentioned in the general study of existence and in first philosophy. There we explained the marks of the Necessary Being and His oneness. We said that, as a concept, “existent” divides into necessary and possible. A possible thing, in itself, is no more likely to exist than not to exist. It therefore needs something outside itself to make it exist. If it made itself more likely to exist, then it would be necessary in itself, though we had assumed it was possible. The same applies if it made its own nonexistence more likely: it would then be impossible, though we had assumed it was possible. This is a contradiction. So the Necessary Being must exist. Since things exist, either one of them is necessary—in which case the point is admitted—or we must reach the Necessary Being, because the chain cannot continue without end, as we have already shown. A circle also leads to an endless chain, and is impossible; it would also make a thing come before itself, which is clearly impossible.
Station One: The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness

The fact that the cause is considered under different descriptions does not remove this problem. Different descriptions do not make the thing itself into two things. A circle still leads to an endless chain and makes a thing come before itself. This path comes closer than most to the path of the people of truth, but it is not the same path, despite what some have claimed. The people of truth consider the reality of existence. Here, the argument starts from the concept “existent.” In brief, the idea of “existent” shows that it cannot be real unless the Necessary Being exists. If every existent were only possible, then nothing could exist at all. A possible thing either exists without a cause, which is obviously impossible, or it exists because of something else. If that other thing is also possible, then either the chain continues without end, forms a circle, or leads to the Necessary Being. The first two choices are impossible, and the third contradicts the assumption that every existent is possible. Yet it must be true, since it is impossible for all possible things to exist without the Necessary Being. This is what Avicenna called the path of the people of truth, and later thinkers followed him.
